summary: The CLI's Drizzle migration sweep now matches the whole eql_v3_* domain family, schema-qualified tables and extra mangled forms; it is now also run by `stash eql migration --drizzle`, not only by `eql install --drizzle`. Matched sibling migrations are rewritten on disk into ADD+DROP+RENAME, which is DROP+ADD and loses the column's data. Before this change a v3 user's in-place ALTER failed at migrate time. Now the file is turned into runnable SQL that drops the column, with a header comment and a log line as the only guard. The sweep only sees the target type, not the source type. So an encrypted-to-encrypted v3 domain change (for example eql_v3_text_eq to eql_v3_text_search) is rewritten the same way and would drop already-encrypted data. Whether Postgres would have accepted the original jsonb-domain-to-jsonb-domain ALTER is unverified. Regex coverage in the unit tests is extensive, but nothing tests against a real Postgres. No tests were run and no CI results were available. The wizard's copy of the rewriter stays v2-only by design (documented).

behaviour_changes.description: `stash eql migration --drizzle` (EQL v3 migration-first path) now sweeps every *.sql file in the Drizzle out directory, except the one it just generated, and rewrites matching ALTER COLUMN … SET DATA TYPE <eql domain>; statements in place on disk. At base this command never modified sibling migrations.

The rewrite matcher now recognises eql_v3_[a-z0-9_]+ in addition to eql_v2_encrypted, plus the dotted public.<domain> forms and schema-qualified "schema"."table" names. This applies to both CLI callers, so `eql install --drizzle` also now rewrites v3 statements it previously left alone.

Emitted SQL changed. The ADD COLUMN uses the matched domain instead of a hard-coded eql_v2_encrypted. ADD/DROP/RENAME are now separated by `--> statement-breakpoint`. The commented UPDATE no longer ends in ';'. The header comment now states that the rewrite destroys data on populated tables.

The statement tail tightened from `[^;]*;` to `\s*;`, so an ALTER … SET DATA TYPE <eql> USING …; is no longer rewritten (at base, v2 rewrote it and silently dropped the USING clause). A new broad NEAR_MISS_RE scan reports such statements as `skipped`. Both commands then print a warning and a closing 'sweep did not fully complete' warning. The sweep is still non-fatal.

rewriteEncryptedAlterColumns (CLI module, internal) now returns {rewritten, skipped} instead of string[]. Both in-package callers were updated. The wizard has its own separate copy with the old signature and is unaffected.
The shipped agent skills skills/stash-cli and skills/stash-drizzle now describe the sweep and say it is safe only on empty tables.

failure_scenarios.title: Encrypted-to-encrypted v3 domain change is rewritten into DROP+ADD, losing ciphertext
failure_scenarios.trigger: A user changes an already-encrypted Drizzle column from one v3 domain to another (e.g. adds ordering/search: eql_v3_text_eq → eql_v3_text_search). drizzle-kit emits ALTER … SET DATA TYPE "undefined"."eql_v3_text_search";. The user then runs `stash eql migration --drizzle` or `eql install --drizzle` with that file in the out directory.
failure_scenarios.mechanism: ALTER_COLUMN_TO_ENCRYPTED_RE only captures table, column and target type; the source type is not in the statement, so a domain-to-domain change is indistinguishable from plaintext-to-encrypted. Every match is rewritten into ADD tmp / DROP original / RENAME. v3 domains are CREATE DOMAIN … AS jsonb, so a jsonb-domain to jsonb-domain ALTER may have been runnable as-is if the target domain's CHECK accepts the existing payloads. That would turn a working migration into a destructive one. Unverified: the v3 domain DDL is not in the checkout.
failure_scenarios.consequence: When the migration is applied, the encrypted column on a populated table is dropped and replaced by an all-NULL column. Its ciphertext is unrecoverable without a backup, and the CLI output frames the rewrite as a fix for an unrunnable migration. Tables that never held plaintext are hit, so the header comment, which is written about plaintext columns, is easy to dismiss.

existing_verification.description: Unit tests assert that every v3 domain target is rewritten. None distinguish source type or cover encrypted→encrypted changes.

missing_verification: Run drizzle-kit generate for an eql_v3_text_eq → eql_v3_text_search change and apply the unrewritten ALTER against a Postgres with the EQL v3 bundle and encrypted rows, to establish whether it was runnable before the rewrite.
A test or guard that skips or flags (rather than rewrites) ALTERs whose source column is already an EQL type, e.g. by consulting the drizzle snapshot JSON.
failure_scenarios.mitigation: Use the drizzle snapshot (or a sibling meta/_journal) to tell whether the source column was already an EQL type, and report those statements as `skipped` instead of rewriting them. Otherwise make the rewrite opt-in or interactive whenever a matched statement exists, and document domain-to-domain changes explicitly.

failure_scenarios.title: Loud migrate failure on populated v3 tables becomes silent plaintext loss
failure_scenarios.trigger: A v3 user changes a populated plaintext column to an eql_v3_* domain, runs `stash eql migration --drizzle`, and then runs `drizzle-kit migrate` (as the CLI's Next Steps note instructs) without reading the rewritten file's header. CI/CD pipelines that run migrate automatically are included.
failure_scenarios.mechanism: At base the v3 path left the in-place ALTER untouched, so migrate failed with a cast error and no data changed. At head the sweep rewrites it into ADD+DROP+RENAME, which Postgres accepts. The only guards are SQL comments and an info-level log line. The closing note still says to run drizzle-kit migrate, and the sweep is non-fatal.
failure_scenarios.consequence: The original plaintext column is dropped and the new encrypted column is NULL for every row. Data is lost on the first migrate, in whatever environment runs it, possibly production.

existing_verification.description: migration.test.ts asserts that the sibling is rewritten and that the generated migration is skipped. rewrite-migrations.test.ts asserts the header text. Nothing checks that the user is stopped or asked to confirm.

missing_verification: A decision, recorded in the PR, that auto-rewriting to destructive SQL is preferable to failing loudly for v3 users.
A test that the Next Steps note warns about data loss when files were rewritten (currently it only warns when the sweep is incomplete).
failure_scenarios.mitigation: When `rewritten` is non-empty, raise the log to warn level and change the Next Steps note to say that rewritten files drop data on non-empty tables. Alternatively, require a --rewrite-alters flag or a confirmation prompt before writing.

failure_scenarios.title: Sweep rewrites historical, already-applied migrations in the out directory
failure_scenarios.trigger: The out directory contains an older migration with a v3 SET DATA TYPE statement that was already applied, e.g. against an empty table or a domain-to-domain change. `stash eql migration --drizzle` is then run, for example on an EQL upgrade.
failure_scenarios.mechanism: The sweep iterates every *.sql entry in outDir except the newly generated file and writes changes back unconditionally (rewrite-migrations.ts:147-183). It does not consult the drizzle journal to skip applied migrations, so the history of applied migrations is edited.
failure_scenarios.consequence: Committed migration history diverges from what production ran. Fresh environments replay different DDL (DROP+ADD instead of ALTER), which can lose constraints or indexes, and the diff appears as an unexpected change to old migrations in review.
missing_verification: A test that applied migrations (per meta/_journal.json) are not rewritten.
failure_scenarios.mitigation: Limit the sweep to migrations not yet in the journal, or to files newer than the last applied entry; otherwise list rewritten historical files prominently.

recommended_controls.description: Add an integration test against Postgres with the EQL v3 bundle. It should cover (a) a domain-to-domain ALTER generated by drizzle-kit, showing whether it was runnable unrewritten, and (b) that the rewritten SQL executes.

Reviewer should decide whether rewriting into data-destroying SQL by default is acceptable for the v3 migration-first path. The alternatives are a flag/prompt, or flagging instead of rewriting. The reviewer should also decide whether encrypted→encrypted changes must be excluded.
Escalate the 'Rewrote N files' message to warn and mention data loss in the closing Next Steps note whenever files were rewritten.
Skip migrations already listed in meta/_journal.json, or at least report historical files separately.
Run packages/cli unit tests (rewrite-migrations.test.ts, eql/__tests__/migration.test.ts) in CI before release.

evidence.claim: ENCRYPTED_DOMAIN matches eql_v2_encrypted or any eql_v3_[a-z0-9_]+.
The strict matcher captures schema/table, column and target type only, with a `\s*;` tail. It has no capture for the column's source type.

The v3 migration command now runs rewriteEncryptedAlterColumns over outDir (skipping only the generated file). It logs rewritten files at info level, warns only when skipped/failed, and the Next Steps note still says to run drizzle-kit migrate.
Iterates every .sql file in outDir, writes the rewritten content back with writeFile, and collects near-misses. There is no journal or applied-state check.
The install command consumes {rewritten, skipped} and adds the skipped/incomplete warnings. It uses the same shared matcher, so it now also rewrites v3 forms.
renderSafeAlter emits ADD tmp "public".<domain>, a commented UPDATE, DROP original and RENAME, separated by statement-breakpoints. The header warns of data destruction on populated tables.
NEAR_MISS_RE flags any remaining ';'-terminated statement that contains SET DATA TYPE and an eql_v2/eql_v3 token.
The wizard calls its own v2-only rewriteEncryptedAlterColumns copy with the string[] return shape, which is unaffected by the CLI signature change.
Comment states v3 columns are CREATE DOMAIN … AS jsonb. That is the basis for a domain-to-domain ALTER possibly being castable; it is not confirmed against the SQL bundle.
The shipped skill now documents the --drizzle sweep and its empty-table-only safety.

Unit tests cover all v3 domains, mangled forms, schema-qualified tables, USING near-misses and breakpoints. All are string assertions on files with no source-type, journal or Postgres execution case. Not run.
